chapter: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
title: Movies end the pit orchestras and Black violinists lose work
summary: Milt explains that talking pictures ended the theatre pit bands, putting Black violinists out of work in Chicago and New York.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Now, what I was going to...what I wanted to bring this to here was about Charles Elgar. Now, after this, Charles Elgar didn't get much work. He began to get around to where he didn't get much work. I didn't see him playing any place any more. Now the violins... This is, of course, 1927. The violins are all out of the business. All the Black violin players have lost their jobs because Jolson has made the movie, The Sound Of Jazz [sic] or something, and no more pit bands in the Regal. In Chicago, where you'd have everybody at the Regal, everybody at the Metropolitan Theatre, all these musicians, all of our Black violin players are out of week.
It was sad around New York. They were all hanging around the Amsterdam Club. You'd see them with their fiddles, and they're still rehearsing and everything, but nothing's happening.
Yeah. Well, that's the same thing that happened in Chicago.
